6a(1).fact: Bicycles are legal vehicles that belong on the roadway obeying standard traffic laws because sidewalks present severe collision hazards at driveways and intersections.
6a(1).misconception: Bicyclists should ride on pedestrian sidewalks rather than city streets to avoid traffic dangers during a road safety test.
6a(1).pamphlet_summary: Scouts demonstrate vehicular cycling competencies under counselor observation, confirming mastery of lane positioning, hand signals, and traffic negotiation. Counselors verify that riders operate predictably as drivers of vehicles while scanning for roadway hazards and obeying traffic control devices (p. 36).
6a(1).socratic_question: Why does the law treat a bicycle as a vehicle rather than a pedestrian conveyance when riding on public roads?

6a(1)(a).fact: Turning left from the far right curb cuts across traffic lanes unpredictably and places the cyclist directly in the blind spot of forward-moving vehicles.
6a(1)(a).misconception: Cyclists should always make left turns by hugging the right curb all the way through an intersection.
6a(1)(a).pamphlet_summary: In light traffic, cyclists signal, shoulder check, and merge into the center or left turn pocket to turn like a motor vehicle. During heavy traffic, riders execute an alternate box turn by proceeding straight across the intersection, stopping at the far corner, realigning the bike, and crossing with the green signal (p. 38).
6a(1)(a).socratic_question: When traffic is moving too fast for you to safely merge left into the turn lane, how can you use a two-step box turn to navigate the intersection safely?

6a(1)(b).fact: Rear scanning is essential before a right turn to detect overtaking vehicles, right-turning motorists, and pedestrians stepping off the curb.
6a(1)(b).misconception: Cyclists do not need to check behind them before turning right because they already occupy the right edge of the street.
6a(1)(b).pamphlet_summary: Cyclists must scan behind, signal the turn with an upturned left arm or extended right arm, and yield to crossing pedestrians before turning. The turn must stay tight within the right lane without swinging out wide into adjacent motor vehicle traffic (p. 37).
6a(1)(b).socratic_question: Why is scanning over your left shoulder just as important before making a right turn as it is before making a left turn?

6a(1)(c).fact: Riding straight from inside a right-turn-only lane puts the cyclist on a direct collision course with turning motor vehicles.
6a(1)(c).misconception: Cyclists going straight through an intersection should stay along the far right curb even inside a right-turn-only lane.
6a(1)(c).pamphlet_summary: When approaching an intersection with a dedicated right turn lane, cyclists continuing straight must merge left out of that lane before the intersection. Riders position themselves along the right side of the through lane or in the pocket between lanes to avoid right hooks (p. 39).
6a(1)(c).socratic_question: What danger do you create if you stay pinned against the right curb while riding through an intersection marked exclusively for turning vehicles?

6a(1)(d).fact: Riding inside the door zone leaves zero reaction time to avoid an opening car door, which can cause severe blunt impact or throw a cyclist under overtaking traffic.
6a(1)(d).misconception: Hugging parked car doors as tightly as possible gives moving cars behind more room and keeps the cyclist safe.
6a(1)(d).pamphlet_summary: Cyclists should maintain a steady, straight line roughly three feet from the road edge or curb rather than weaving into empty spaces between parked cars. When passing parallel parked vehicles, riders must track at least four feet away to remain clear of opening car doors (p. 40).
6a(1)(d).socratic_question: Why does weaving in and out of open parking spaces make you harder for approaching drivers to spot and predict?
6a(1)(d).topic_title: Roadside Positioning and Door Zone Safety

6a(1)(e).fact: Approaching tracks diagonally causes the front tire to drop into the flangeway gap between the pavement and steel rail, throwing the rider instantly.
6a(1)(e).misconception: Speeding diagonally across railroad tracks gets the wheels across faster and reduces the chance of falling.
6a(1)(e).pamphlet_summary: Cyclists must steer across railway tracks at a right angle as close to ninety degrees as possible while standing slightly out of the saddle with level pedals. Crossing diagonally risks wedging narrow bike tires into the track flangeway flutes or slipping on wet steel rails (p. 41).
6a(1)(e).socratic_question: How should you adjust your steering path on a road where railroad tracks cross the asphalt at an acute diagonal angle?

6a(2).fact: The requirement mandates structured continuous touring rides on planned routes away from main highways rather than an accumulation of random daily utility trips.
6a(2).misconception: A Scout can combine multiple short neighborhood errands together to calculate total mileage toward the designated tour distances.
6a(2).pamphlet_summary: Scouts build aerobic conditioning and road endurance by completing six distinct tours ranging from ten to twenty-five miles along secondary roads. Each outing requires a written activity log documenting calendar dates, precise course routes, weather observations, and notable milestones (p. 43).
6a(2).socratic_question: How does stepping up your ride distances from ten to fifteen and then twenty-five miles prepare your body and equipment for a fifty-mile trek?

6a(3).fact: The eight-hour time limit is continuous elapsed clock time from departure to return, meaning extended stops reduce available riding time.
6a(3).misconception: The eight-hour cutoff time excludes rest breaks, lunchtime stops, and mechanical repairs.
6a(3).pamphlet_summary: After finishing the preparation rides, Scouts demonstrate advanced cycling stamina by completing a fifty-mile road journey within an eight-hour window. The option allows either executing an independently mapped route along rural backroads or joining a sanctioned century-style group tour (p. 46).
6a(3).socratic_question: What pacing and hydration strategy will keep your average rolling speed high enough to finish fifty miles well within the eight-hour limit?

6a(3)(a).fact: The handbook explicitly directs Scouts away from main highways to minimize exposure to high-speed commercial traffic and dangerous interchange ramps.
6a(3)(a).misconception: Fast state highways with wide paved shoulders are preferable because they offer the most direct route for a fifty-mile ride.
6a(3)(a).pamphlet_summary: The Scout designs a fifty-mile circuit on secondary or country roads, mapping elevation profiles, water resupply locations, and rest zones. Navigating with the map, the cyclist rides the planned route while maintaining an average pace sufficient to finish inside eight hours (p. 47).
6a(3)(a).socratic_question: What topographic and logistical factors should you evaluate on a paper or digital map before deciding on a fifty-mile route?

6a(3)(b).fact: Organized tour riders must track cue sheet instructions independently to navigate safely and fulfill the post-ride mapping requirement.
6a(3)(b).misconception: Riding in an organized group event means the cyclist does not need to pay attention to turns or route directions.
6a(3)(b).pamphlet_summary: Scouts register for and ride in an organized bicycle tour of fifty miles or more, adhering to ride marshals and support stop schedules within eight hours. Following the ride, the Scout translates the printed turn-by-turn cue sheet into an accurate drawn route map (p. 48).
6a(3)(b).socratic_question: How does converting an event cue sheet with turn mileage into a detailed map help you understand how large-scale road tours are organized?

6b(1).fact: Effective off-road handling depends on loose limbs acting as shock absorbers and allowing the bicycle to move independently beneath the torso.
6b(1).misconception: Mountain bike handling relies strictly on stiff arm strength to force the handlebars wherever the trail goes.
6b(1).pamphlet_summary: Mountain bike handling requires active dynamic balance, proactive cadence management, and calculated body positioning over varied off-road terrain. Riders demonstrate core body positions, smooth gear shifts ahead of steep trail grades, and weighted wheel control on ascents and descents (p. 52).
6b(1).socratic_question: Why is dynamic body-bike separation more effective for keeping balance on rocky trails than sitting rigidly in the saddle?

6b(1)(a).fact: Leaning the bike into the turn while keeping the body upright presses the aggressive side knobs of the trail tires into the dirt for maximum cornering grip.
6b(1)(a).misconception: A cyclist should lean their entire body and head at the exact same angle as the bicycle when taking tight dirt turns.
6b(1)(a).pamphlet_summary: Riders switch between a relaxed neutral stance for coasting and an aggressive ready position with bent elbows and dropped heels for rough terrain. During cornering, riders lean the bicycle frame underneath them while keeping the torso upright and weighting the outside downward pedal for tire traction (p. 54).
6b(1)(a).socratic_question: How does keeping your outside foot pressed down at the six o'clock position help stabilize your mountain bike through a loose dirt berm?

6b(1)(b).fact: Shifting under heavy chain tension causes chain suck, missed shifts, and mechanical breakage that stalls the climb.
6b(1)(b).misconception: Waiting to downshift until your pedals grind to a near halt on a steep hill produces the most climbing torque.
6b(1)(b).pamphlet_summary: Trail riders anticipate grade changes by downshifting into an easier gear before the slope steepens or before clearing an obstacle. Shifting requires easing pedal pressure momentarily during gear transitions to avoid snapping chains or stripping drivetrain teeth (p. 56).
6b(1)(b).socratic_question: What chain and derailleur sounds warn you that you waited too long to downshift on a steep dirt incline?

6b(1)(c).fact: Standing straight up unweights the rear tire, causing it to spin out uselessly on loose rocks or dirt surfaces.
6b(1)(c).misconception: Standing straight up and pedaling as hard as possible is the best way to conquer a steep loose-rock trail climb.
6b(1)(c).pamphlet_summary: On steep climbs, riders shift body weight forward over the handlebars and crouch while keeping tire traction on the ground. On descents, riders stand out of the saddle, shift hips behind the seat, keep pedals level, and feather both brakes to prevent pitching over the front wheel (p. 58).
6b(1)(c).socratic_question: Where should your center of gravity be positioned relative to the saddle when descending a steep, rutted trail drop?

6b(2).fact: Bicyclists must always yield the trail to hikers and equestrians, and downhill riders must yield to uphill cyclists who have the right of way.
6b(2).misconception: Downhill mountain bikers have the right of way over uphill cyclists and hikers because of their higher speed and momentum.
6b(2).pamphlet_summary: Scouts demonstrate courteous shared-use trail protocols by slowing down, communicating audibly, and yielding to hikers and equestrians. The test also requires executing obstacle-clearing techniques such as unweighting wheels or lofting the front wheel over rocks and fallen logs (p. 60).
6b(2).socratic_question: Why do established trail rules require downhill mountain bikers to stop and yield to cyclists climbing up the trail?

6b(2)(a).fact: Climbing riders always retain the right of way because restarting momentum on a steep incline is far more difficult than braking while rolling downhill.
6b(2)(a).misconception: Downhill cyclists have the right of way over climbing riders because high speed makes braking on a descent harder.
6b(2)(a).pamphlet_summary: Mountain bikers yield the trail to hikers and pack stock, always slowing to a walking pace and giving a friendly vocal greeting before passing. Downhill cyclists must yield to climbing riders because the uphill rider requires continuous pedaling cadence to maintain balance and traction (p. 52).
6b(2)(a).socratic_question: If you are descending a narrow singletrack trail at speed and see a rider struggling up the hill toward you, what should you do and why?

6b(2)(b).fact: A rider must rise into the standing ready position and shift weight backward while applying a pedal punch to float the front wheel cleanly across the hazard.
6b(2)(b).misconception: Pulling straight upward on the handlebars while seated in the saddle is the proper way to lift a front wheel over a trail obstacle.
6b(2)(b).pamphlet_summary: Riders approach trail obstacles in the attack position with level pedals and bent elbows, using a pedal punch or front-wheel lift to roll over logs. When an obstacle exceeds personal skill or tire clearance, cyclists dismount on the uphill side and walk the bicycle across or around the hazard (p. 54).
6b(2)(b).socratic_question: When you encounter a fallen log across the path that is taller than your chainring, how do you decide whether to roll over it or dismount?

6b(2)(c).fact: Sudden front braking on loose or slick surfaces causes the front wheel to tuck and skid, requiring riders to feather the rear brake instead.
6b(2)(c).misconception: Grabbing the front brake lever helps stabilize the bicycle when steering through loose gravel or wet roots.
6b(2)(c).pamphlet_summary: Cyclists maintain steady momentum, keep pedals level in the neutral standing position, and cross wet roots and rocks at a perpendicular ninety-degree angle to avoid slipping. In loose gravel, riders stay off the front brake and steer gently with the hips to prevent the front wheel from washing out (p. 55).
6b(2)(c).socratic_question: Why can hitting an exposed, wet tree root at a sharp diagonal angle cause your wheels to slide out from underneath you?

6b(3).fact: Tires cut deep ruts into saturated soil that funnel water runoff into destructive erosion gullies and ruin the tread surface.
6b(3).misconception: Riding across saturated muddy trails is harmless because drying dirt naturally smooths over bicycle tracks.
6b(3).pamphlet_summary: Trail riding rules follow the International Mountain Bicycling Association guidelines to ride open trails, leave no trace, control the bicycle, yield respectfully, never scare animals, and plan ahead. A trail is unsuitable for riding when standing water or saturated soil creates mud, meaning bicycle tires leave ruts that channel runoff and cause severe erosion (p. 56).
6b(3).socratic_question: How can riding on a trail twenty-four hours after a heavy downpour permanently damage the trail bed for other users?

6b(4).fact: Each mileage target must be performed as an independent training session so the rider progressively builds off-road stamina and bike handling skill.
6b(4).misconception: Scouts can combine the two separate 5-mile rides into a single 10-mile outing to fulfill the requirement faster.
6b(4).pamphlet_summary: Scouts build endurance and bike handling progressively by completing six separate trail outings spanning two 2-mile, two 5-mile, and two 8-mile rides before tackling longer distances. Each ride report requires documenting the specific calendar date, approved trail system, distance, weather conditions, mechanical issues, and natural or historical sights observed along the way (p. 58).
6b(4).socratic_question: Why does the Cycling merit badge require you to start with two-mile rides and gradually increase to eight miles instead of jumping straight to the twenty-two-mile trek?

6b(5).fact: The trip must be completed in its entirety during a single day to demonstrate the endurance developed through the preparatory rides.
6b(5).misconception: Splitting the twenty-two miles across two consecutive days satisfies the requirement as long as the total route distance is achieved.
6b(5).pamphlet_summary: After finishing all progressive training rides, the Scout plots a continuous 22-mile trail expedition on topographic or trail park maps, connecting multiple trail networks while avoiding heavily trafficked highways. The Scout must follow this custom map to complete the entire route within a single day while managing hydration, nutrition, and trailside repair readiness (p. 60).
6b(5).socratic_question: When mapping out a twenty-two-mile trail journey across unfamiliar parks, how do you verify that your planned connectors keep you off dangerous highways?
